leadership_examples.title: Disciplined AI-assisted development workflow (with a caught AI bug as evidence)
leadership_examples.situation: Regular use of AI coding tools (ChatGPT, Copilot, Junie, Codespaces assistant, Muse) for breakdown, planning, boilerplate, and debugging.
leadership_examples.actions: Treats AI like a very junior dev: breaks work into tiny pieces, hands over one piece at a time, code-reviews and tests each piece before moving on; never treats generated code as authoritative.

Subject caught it the next day rehearsing a demo walkthrough out loud, fixed it, and added varied-date test data so that class of mistake cannot hide again.

leadership_examples.title: Leading the ES8 migration — architecture simplification, comparison testing, and a documented lesson learned
leadership_examples.situation: Multiple databases (ES7, PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB) caused scalability/reliability issues; ES7-to-ES8 upgrade affected essentially every API endpoint; the ES7 library was incompatible with ES8.
leadership_examples.actions: Coordinated ~7-8 engineers across teams; pushed for the simplest architecture (including separating bulk delivery into its own tool, ACC-025); refactored the API for ES8 and rewrote queries in a new library; helped design request-comparison tooling (results + latency) between old and new implementations.
leadership_examples.reasoning: Consolidate to a single source of truth, keep the architecture simple, and earn confidence in behavior preservation empirically rather than by assumption.
leadership_examples.outcome: Migration completed in 2-3 months with zero downtime; TimescaleDB retired, cutting infrastructure cost. Lesson subject stated he would apply next time: invest earlier in documenting existing behavior and building migration-comparison tooling.

The assistant did not re-read every raw transcript message of every prior conversation; where memory notes summarize a conversation, the summary was treated as the available evidence and items are labeled accordingly. Nothing was invented to fill gaps.

An earlier assistant draft (Beacon application, pre-2026-10-19) wrongly stated Go was learned at GreyNoise and Scala at Capital One. Subject corrected it 2026-10-19: Scala learned at IQVIA/Wingspan, Go learned at Capital One. This inventory uses the CORRECTED version everywhere and flags the old version here so a future importer does not resurrect it.

Some tailored resumes describe 'building data/detection pipelines'. Subject corrected this 2026-10-09: he did NOT own/build the data pipeline (pipeline team owned ES indices and Kafka topics); he owned the public API + data delivery reading from them, and oversaw the ES migration at planning level. This inventory uses the corrected framing.

RESOLVED 2026-10-20 by subject: during the GreyNoise years he used his PERSONAL GitHub account, so private GreyNoise contributions ARE included in his personal profile counts (~790 over four years: 2023: 157, 2024: 397, 2025: 171; 67 in the past year). Before GreyNoise, most employers gave him a separate GitHub account, so contributions from those accounts are NOT reflected in his personal profile — the counts therefore represent mainly the GreyNoise era and underrepresent earlier employers. Safe external framing: counts reflect personal-account activity including private GreyNoise work; earlier employers' work lived on separate accounts.

No former legal name, no assigned-gender information, no family members' private details, and no confidential employer-dispute details were included. Work-authorization facts are included only because the subject explicitly provides them on applications.
